n: Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished
who: Gynaecologist Eduardo Vela
d: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987. It was the first trial in Spain over the 'stolen babies' of the Franco era and after. A judge had recorded about 30,000 cases of Spanish children taken, according to the report.

n: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cover: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.
d: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.

n: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
who: Focus on Children, Utah agency run by Scott and Karen Banks
d: Samoan parents were told their children would go to the US temporarily for schooling, but the children were adopted permanently. A federal indictment on 28 February 2007 charged Scott and Karen Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. All pleaded guilty on 6 January 2009 to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; in February 2009 Judge David Sam sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.

n: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
d: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

n: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
d: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.

n: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
d: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

n: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
d: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

n: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
d: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.

n: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
d: The Ideal Maternity Home in Nova Scotia, run by William and Lila Young from the late 1920s until 1947, promised discreet birthing and adoption for unmarried mothers. According to author Bette Cahill, people paid up to $10,000, usually disguised as a donation, to adopt babies from the home, while babies considered 'unmarketable' were fed only molasses and water; many died and were buried in butter boxes. Wikipedia, citing Cahill, adds that mothers were charged $500, that the provincial Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934, and that the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act; a 1946 Montreal Standard article described their 'baby farm rackets'.

n: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
d: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

n: Colombia — 1981 ring selling Andean children abroad with forged papers
who: Adoption trafficking ring
d: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. In 2003 Interpol issued a detention order for the manager of an uncertified Costa Rica-based adoption agency suspected of trafficking babies from Colombia in 2000–2002 (suspect, not convicted).

n: North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'
place: Clwyd and Gwynedd, North Wales (Bryn Estyn, Wrexham, among others)
who: Clwyd and Gwynedd county councils' children's homes, incl. Bryn Estyn; North Wales Police criticised
cover: The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.
d: Sir Ronald Waterhouse's tribunal took evidence from about 650 people who had been in care and published 'Lost in Care' in February 2000, finding widespread abuse over about 20 years in children's homes in North Wales. Allegations were reported across almost 40 homes, with the report concentrating on seven. Seven former care workers were convicted after a 1991 police inquiry, five of them from Bryn Estyn. The report found responses were 'too little and too late' and that children's interests were sacrificed to protect professional positions; officers of North Wales Police were among those accused.

n: Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA
place: Lambeth, London (Shirley Oaks home located near Croydon)
who: London Borough of Lambeth; Shirley Oaks, South Vale and Angell Road children's homes
cover: Over 40 years only one senior employee was disciplined. The council did not tell a coroner that a boy found dead at Shirley Oaks in 1977 had alleged sexual abuse by his 'house father' Donald Hosegood; the inquiry asked the Metropolitan Police to consider a criminal investigation into this.
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 27 July 2021 that children in Lambeth's care were subjected to decades of cruelty and sexual abuse from the 1960s. By June 2020 the council had complaints from 705 former residents; at Shirley Oaks, allegations were made against 177 staff or associated people involving at least 529 former residents. At Angell Road, children including some under five were systematically exposed to sexual abuse. The inquiry found racism, nepotism, corruption and mismanagement in the council, and that most children at Shirley Oaks (1980) and South Vale (1990–91) were Black.

n: Kendall House girls' home, Gravesend — Proctor review
who: Kendall House, a Church of England children's home taking girls placed by social services
d: An independent review chaired by Dr Sue Proctor, commissioned by the Bishop of Rochester and published in July 2016, found that from 1967 girls as young as 11 were routinely given antidepressants, sedatives and antipsychotics, sometimes without medical assessment. Former residents were physically, emotionally and sometimes sexually abused, including two rapes while girls were held in isolation. The review heard from 20 former residents and examined records of 44. A 1980 television programme had already exposed the home.

n: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers
place: West Berlin (network nodes also in Göttingen, Hannover, Lüneburg, Tübingen, Heppenheim)
who: Berlin Senate youth administration and state youth office (Landesjugendamt); sexologist Helmut Kentler (Pädagogisches Zentrum Berlin, later TU Hannover); network incl. Gerold Becker of the Odenwaldschule
cover: University of Hildesheim researchers found the abuse was carried out and institutionalised under the responsibility of the Landesjugendamt and the Berlin Senate administration; Kentler died in 2008 without prosecution.
d: From the late 1960s (Kentler held a post at the Senate's Pädagogisches Zentrum from 1967 to 1976) West Berlin youth authorities, on the advice of Helmut Kentler, placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, as a form of 'resocialisation'. University of Hildesheim reports (2020 and final report 22 February 2024) reconstructed a nationwide network in science, youth welfare and administration that supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions and sexual violence, continuing beyond 2000. Some children were about five years old when placed. Berlin says known victims have received compensation.

n: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
d: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.

n: Godhavn Report — Danish state children's homes 1945–1976
place: Godhavn boys' home, Tisvilde, North Zealand (and 18 other state homes)
who: Danish state-run children's homes incl. Godhavn boys' home
d: The Godhavn Report, published 9 May 2011, examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976, finding neglect, physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22% of Godhavn residents had been given psychiatric drugs by psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld. No prosecutions followed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims in 2019.

n: France — children in state child welfare (ASE) exploited in prostitution
place: France (cases raised in Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne)
who: Aide sociale à l'enfance (departmental child welfare services)
d: A French parliamentary commission of inquiry report published in April 2025 estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services (ASE), which hold about 396,900 minors, are victims of prostitution. Lawyers asked the Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne departments for administrative reviews over children in care who were prostituted; teenagers are often housed in hotels with little supervision. A complaint was filed with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.

n: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children — Restorative Inquiry
who: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children (provincially funded orphanage for Black children)
d: Former residents of the home, which operated from 1921, described neglect and emotional, physical and sexual abuse. A class action was settled and the provincial government apologised in 2014 to former residents and the African Nova Scotian community for harm caused by systemic racism. The Restorative Inquiry delivered its final report on 28 November 2019 in Halifax.

n: Boy Scouts of America — 82,000+ abuse claims and bankruptcy settlement
who: Boy Scouts of America (now Scouting America) and local councils
cover: BSA kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers; 1,247 files from 1965–1985 were ordered released by the Oregon Supreme Court in June 2012 after a 2010 civil jury award of nearly $20 million.
d: BSA filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2020. By the November 2020 claims deadline more than 82,000 people had filed sexual abuse claims, which lawyers said was larger than all Catholic Church cases combined. A $2.46 billion settlement trust pays survivors between $3,500 and $2.7 million; the US Supreme Court declined to review the plan in January 2026. BSA's internal 'ineligible volunteer' files, which the Oregon Supreme Court ordered largely released in 2012, recorded suspected abusers over decades.

n: Texas foster care — federal court finds 'rape and over-medication were the norm'
place: Texas (case heard in Corpus Christi federal court)
who: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services; Health and Human Services Commission
cover: Judge Jack held Texas in contempt three times (2019, 2020, April 2024) for failing to investigate abuse complaints and protect children; in 2019 she said she could no longer find the department credible.
d: In a class action filed in 2011 on behalf of children in long-term state care, US District Judge Janis Graham Jack ruled in December 2015 that Texas violated foster children's constitutional rights by placing them in a system where 'rape and over-medication were the norm'. She later ordered 24-hour awake supervision and flagging of children who were victims or perpetrators of sexual violence. In April 2024 she found the state in contempt for a third time and fined it $100,000 a day over failures to investigate abuse reports.

n: Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario)
place: Ontario (13 training schools incl. Pine Ridge, Bowmanville; Hillcrest, Guelph; Brookside, Cobourg; Cecil Facer, Sudbury)
who: Government of Ontario provincial training schools (juvenile reformatories)
d: In the class action Brown v. Ontario, the province agreed to a settlement of up to CAD 60 million, signed 21 January 2026 and approved by the Ontario Superior Court on 21 May 2026, for former residents of 13 provincial training schools between 1953 and 1984. It covers physical and sexual assault and solitary confinement. Ontario denies liability and the court did not decide the merits.

n: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
d: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.

n: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cover: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.
d: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.

n: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cover: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.
d: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.

n: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cover: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.
d: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.

n: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
place: Romania (incl. Siret children's psychiatric hospital; Sighetu Marmației institution)
who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
d: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.

n: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinder (VCP) — independent study of sexualised violence
who: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (VCP), Protestant scouting federation
cover: The study found 'old cases' from the 1980s and 1990s were long ignored for lack of any idea of reappraisal (Aufarbeitung).
d: A study by the Munich Institut für Praxisforschung und Projektberatung (IPP) and the Dissens Institute, presented in Kassel on 27 January 2026, found at least 344 people had suffered sexualised violence within the VCP since 1973. It drew on 79 interviews and about 1,300 pages of files on 100 cases. About 60% of victims were girls, two-thirds were aged 13–17 when it began, nearly half the acts occurred after 2000, and more than half on camps or trips. Perpetrators came mostly from within the organisation, often adult group leaders.

n: Haiti — orphanage assessment identifies 3,019 potential trafficking victims
who: Private orphanages in Haiti; Institut du Bien-Être Social et de Recherches (IBESR)
d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. IBESR closed eight non-compliant orphanages in the reporting period and expanded foster care to 121 accredited families to reduce children's vulnerability to trafficking.

n: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
cover: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.
d: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.

n: Panama — legislative subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters
who: Private and NGO shelters (albergues) under the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf)
cover: The Ombudsman found 70% of 44 shelters inspected lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.
d: A National Assembly subcommission report in early February 2021 found cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. By March 2021 the Public Ministry had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected.

n: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
place: Chile (incl. a home in Arica; Punta Arenas)
who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
cover: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.
d: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.

n: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
place: Martissant and other contingent locations, Port-au-Prince
who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cover: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
d: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.

n: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
place: Central African Republic (deployment areas incl. Ouaka)
who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
d: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

n: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
d: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.

n: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
place: AMISOM base camp and Burundian contingent base, Mogadishu
who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
d: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

n: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified)
who: Ethiopian National Defence Forces, Eritrean Defence Forces, Amhara forces and Tigrayan forces
d: The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (October 2022) documented Tigrayan forces' rapes of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021, alongside widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at Mekelle health facilities as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 attributed to the ENDF.

n: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October
place: Gaza Strip, West Bank and southern Israel
who: Israeli security forces (detention and arrest); Hamas and other armed groups (7 October)
d: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. It also found sexual violence was committed on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage. Recorded only to the extent of these UN findings.

n: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
place: Government Science Secondary School, Kankara, Katsina
who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
d: On the night of Friday 11 December 2020 heavily armed gunmen raided the all-boys Government Science Secondary School in Kankara, Katsina state, where more than 800 students lived. The military said 333 pupils were unaccounted for. In an audio message a man identifying himself as Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction; Nigerian officials attributed it to bandits, and the BBC later described a local gang leader as the mastermind of the kidnapping of about 300 boys. The boys were freed within about a week.

n: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07)
place: Colombia (Bloque Oriental and Bloque Sur areas)
who: Former FARC-EP secretariat and commanders
d: The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's Case 07 investigates the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP; in August 2021 it identified a provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims and has accredited 9,854. The JEP indicted former FARC-EP commanders for war crimes including the recruitment and use of children and sexual violence against children, and has referred a former FARC member accused of reproductive violence against recruited girls to its investigation unit. Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility.

n: DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024)
who: M23 (68), CODECO (63), FARDC (47), Raia Mutomboki, Nyatura, ADF and others
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. In 2022 it verified sexual violence against 284 children aged 4 to 17, 56 of them by FARDC.

n: Burkina Faso — abduction of children by JNIM, ISGS and state auxiliaries (UN verified)
who: JNIM, ISGS, Defence and Security Forces / Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP)
d: The UN verified the abduction of 309 children in Burkina Faso in 2024 by JNIM (157), ISGS (80), unidentified perpetrators (47) and the Defence and Security Forces/VDP (25), and the rape of four girls, two by the VDP. In 2022 it verified the rape of 16 girls, 2 by the Defence and Security Forces.

n: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified)
who: Taliban de facto authorities
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children (6 boys, 6 girls) in Afghanistan in 2023, 10 attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence purposes. It verified 13 cases in 2022 (Taliban 7) and 6 in 2024 (Taliban 5).

n: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
place: Colonia Dignidad (now Villa Baviera), Parral, Maule region
kind: sexual abuse + forced labour + child removal
who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cover: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.
d: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.

n: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
d: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

n: Iraq — abduction of children by Da'esh and HPG/PKK (UN verified 2022–2024)
who: Da'esh; HPG/PKK
d: The UN verified the abduction of 18 children in Iraq in 2022, 10 by Da'esh and 4 by HPG/PKK, and of 8 children in 2024 (2 boys by Da'esh, 6 girls by HPG/PKK), mostly for recruitment and use.

n: Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor
place: Manhattan, New York (trial); offences in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, London
who: Ghislaine Maxwell
cover: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche interviewed Maxwell with limited immunity; on 1 Aug 2025 she was moved to the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp Bryan, Texas. A DOJ official recorded secretly said the transfer was against policy (DOJ said he had no role).
d: Maxwell was arrested on 2 July 2020 in Bradford, New Hampshire. On 29 December 2021 a jury convicted her on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor; she was acquitted of enticing a minor to travel. She was sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction on 17 Sept 2024 and the US Supreme Court declined her appeal on 6 Oct 2025; she had argued Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement shielded co-conspirators. As of mid-2026 her lawyer said he would seek a pardon; Blanche said in May 2026 he would not recommend one.

n: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor — civil settlement, loss of titles, 2026 arrest (misconduct in public office)
who: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (formerly Prince Andrew, Duke of York)
cover: Settled civil case with no admission of liability (Feb 2022). In Oct 2025 it was alleged he asked a protection officer to investigate his accuser; the Metropolitan Police took no further action.
d: Virginia Giuffre's court filings from 2014 alleged Epstein trafficked her to Andrew as a minor; he denies it. She sued in New York in Aug 2021; the case settled in Feb 2022 without admission (reported as about £12m). In Oct–Nov 2025 King Charles removed his remaining titles, including 'prince' (letters patent, Nov 2025). On 19 Feb 2026 Thames Valley Police arrested him on suspicion of misconduct in public office over reports from the DOJ files that he sent confidential trade-envoy reports to Epstein in 2010; he was released under investigation the same day. No sexual-offence charge exists; he denies wrongdoing; the investigation is ongoing.

n: Epstein Files Transparency Act and DOJ releases (2025–2026)
who: US Department of Justice; FBI; House Oversight Committee
cover: DOJ said it identified about 6 million potentially responsive pages but released about 3.5 million, withholding about 200,000 under privilege, abuse material and victim-identity grounds; critics in both parties said it broke the law. Faulty redactions exposed at least 43 victims' names (WSJ). The DOJ Inspector General opened a compliance review in April 2026.
d: A 7 July 2025 DOJ/FBI memo said there was no incriminating 'client list', no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent people, and that his death was suicide; it also said Epstein 'harmed over one thousand victims'. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act 427–1 in the House and by unanimous consent in the Senate, and it was signed on 19 Nov 2025. DOJ began releasing files on 19 Dec 2025 and on 30 Jan 2026 published over 3 million more pages (about 3.5 million in total), saying notable individuals were not redacted and warning that the release may include fake or false material submitted by the public. On 5 Mar 2026, after an NPR investigation found pages had been withheld, DOJ published 16 more pages. The releases documented Epstein's continued contact with prominent people after 2008 and led to police inquiries and resignations abroad; they did not establish a client list.

n: Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals
place: Leeds General Infirmary, Stoke Mandeville, Broadmoor and other NHS sites
who: NHS hospitals (Leeds General Infirmary, Stoke Mandeville, Broadmoor and others)
d: Kate Lampard's lessons-learned report (26 February 2015) drew on 44 NHS investigation reports — 28 published in June 2014 and 16 more alongside her report — and found Savile's known victims in NHS hospitals were aged five to 75, including patients, staff and visitors; his status gave him keys and virtually unfettered access to wards. At Leeds General Infirmary 64 people came forward and 60 alleged abuse on the premises, between 1962 and 2009, including three rapes.

n: IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring')
who: Parliament; political parties; police; Director of Public Prosecutions
cover: The inquiry concluded that "deference to class and power was the overriding motive" for decisions in the Montagu and Hayman cases, and that the police showed "a patronising attitude" towards a working-class victim in the Montagu case.
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse examined how Parliament, political parties, the police, prosecutors and the honours system dealt with allegations of child sexual abuse involving people connected to Westminster, and reported on 25 February 2020. It found "no evidence to suggest an organised network of abusers in Westminster". It did find "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people", that the diplomat Sir Peter Hayman "was the beneficiary of preferential, differential and unduly deferential treatment", that party whips' offices were "concerned above all to protect the image of their party" though there was no evidence they deliberately suppressed specific information, that the former Liberal leader David Steel "yielded to considerations of political expediency" over Cyril Smith, and that the honours system in some instances "prioritised reputation and discretion with little or no regard for victims".

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — elite boarding schools (Fettes, Loretto, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston)
who: Fettes College, Loretto School, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston Castle School
cover: Fettes dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa.
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, launched in 2015 and led by Lady Smith, has heard evidence of abuse at elite independent schools including Edinburgh Academy, Fettes College, Gordonstoun, Loretto and Merchiston; Gordonstoun has apologised to anyone abused in its care. Former teacher Iain Wares, accused by scores of former pupils of Edinburgh Academy and Fettes, where he taught in the 1960s and 1970s, admitted in South African extradition documents that he had touched students inappropriately at Edinburgh Academy. South Africa approved the UK's extradition request in 2020 and the Cape Town High Court ruled in 2024 that he could be extradited on three charges; in October 2025 he was arrested in South Africa on a further 90 charges. He has not been tried.

n: Gabriel Matzneff — writer's published accounts of abusing minors
who: Gabriel Matzneff (author); French literary establishment (Gallimard and others)
cover: Literary tolerance: Matzneff published diaries describing sex with minors and child sex tourism in the Philippines (e.g. 1985) and was celebrated on TV (Apostrophes, 1990).
d: From the 1960s Matzneff wrote openly about sex with adolescents and was feted by the Paris literary world. In the memoir 'Le Consentement' (published January 2020) its author, a publishing executive, described their relationship when she was 14. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation for rape of a minor in January 2020, and Gallimard withdrew his journals from sale. The BBC noted that, given the time elapsed, the case was unlikely to lead to charges. In November 2023 prosecutors opened a second investigation after another woman accused him of raping her as a child. He has not been convicted.

n: Sebastian Edathy (Bundestag) — images of naked minors; case closed on payment
who: Sebastian Edathy (SPD member of the Bundestag)
cover: Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich resigned on 14 Feb 2014 after being accused of disclosing the investigation to SPD leaders.
d: Edathy gave up his Bundestag seat in February 2014, and his homes and offices were then searched; Hanover prosecutors said he had placed nine orders for 31 products with a company in Canada. On 2 March 2015, at his trial before the Verden regional court, his lawyer admitted on his behalf that he had downloaded videos and images of naked boys using his official laptop, and the court ended the case against a €5,000 payment to the children's charity Kinderschutzbund; he has no criminal record from it, and he said afterwards that his statement was not a confession.

n: Larry Nassar — USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University
who: Larry Nassar (team doctor); USA Gymnastics; Michigan State University; FBI; US Olympic & Paralympic Committee
cover: Athletes complained as early as 1997. USAG was told on 17 June 2015. The DOJ Inspector General (July 2021) found FBI agents failed to act on the gymnasts' reports and that supervisory agent W. Jay Abbott later lied about it. MSU dean William Strampel was convicted of misconduct in office (2019); charges against ex-MSU president Lou Anna Simon (dismissed 2020) and ex-USAG CEO Steve Penny (dropped 2022) did not end in convictions; coach Kathie Klages's conviction was overturned (2021). USA Gymnastics had complaints against 54 coaches 1996–2006.
d: Nassar pleaded guilty to federal child-abuse-image charges (60 years, Dec 2017) and to criminal sexual conduct in two Michigan counties, receiving 40–175 years in Ingham County (Jan 2018) and 40–125 years in Eaton County (Feb 2018); by the final hearing the number of identified victims had reached 265. Settlements: Michigan State University $500m to more than 300 women and girls (2018); USA Gymnastics and the USOPC $380m (2021); the US government $138.7m to 139 claimants over FBI failures to investigate promptly (April 2024). The Indianapolis Star's September 2016 investigation triggered the case.

n: R. Kelly — racketeering and child sexual abuse material convictions
who: Robert Kelly (singer) and his entourage (racketeering enterprise)
cover: He was acquitted in 2008 of child pornography charges brought in 2002, despite Chicago Sun-Times reporting from 2000.
d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Kelly on 27 Sept 2021 of racketeering, including acts of bribery and sexual exploitation of a child, and of Mann Act sex-trafficking offences; he was sentenced to 30 years. In September 2022 a Chicago federal jury convicted him of three counts of producing child sexual abuse material and three of enticing a minor; in February 2023 he was sentenced to 20 years, 19 of them to run concurrently with the New York term. The 2019 documentary 'Surviving R. Kelly' led to the new prosecutions.

n: 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria
who: Online conspiracy theory targeting Democratic politicians
d: In Oct–Nov 2016 online posts, citing leaked Podesta emails, falsely claimed that the Comet Ping Pong pizzeria in Washington was home to a child sex-abuse ring involving top Democrats. No victims or evidence emerged. On 4 Dec 2016 Edgar Maddison Welch fired an AR-15 rifle inside to 'investigate'; he pleaded guilty in March 2017 to federal assault with a dangerous weapon and transporting a firearm across state lines, and was sentenced to four years in June 2017.

n: Kasur child abuse video scandal (Hussain Khanwala)
who: Local gang filming abuse of children; Punjab police; local MPA (alleged)
cover: Punjab police and the local PML-N provincial assembly member Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan were alleged to have tried to cover it up; the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police clashed with protesting villagers on 8 Aug 2015.
d: In August 2015 it emerged that in Hussain Khanwala village, Kasur district, a gang had filmed the sexual abuse of children and blackmailed their parents by threatening to leak the videos. Pakistani media put the number of children at 280 to 300; the joint investigation team set up by the Punjab government confirmed 19 genuine complaints, examined 47 video clips and charged 17 people (Express Tribune, 14 November 2015). Police, who had failed to act despite pleas from parents, made arrests only after clashes between relatives and authorities drew media attention. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment; Arab News reported in February 2018 that 12 other accused men were acquitted.

n: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples
who: T.B. Joshua; Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN)
d: A BBC Africa Eye investigation published on 8 January 2024 reported corroborating testimony from more than 25 former disciples from seven countries that TB Joshua, founder of the Synagogue Church of All Nations in Lagos, had sexually assaulted and raped followers and subjected them to abuse including solitary confinement, with the most recent experiences in 2019. One woman said he first raped her when she was 17 and that she was made to have forced abortions. Joshua died in June 2021. The church did not respond to the BBC's allegations but has called previous claims unsubstantiated. No official finding. Religious figure placed here for celebrity and political influence.

n: Suffolk County grand jury — Diocese of Rockville Centre (2003)
place: Rockville Centre, Long Island, New York
who: Catholic Diocese of Rockville Centre
cover: Accused priests moved from parish to parish; a diocesan 'intervention team' and legal-affairs team used to silence victims and suppress claims; secret archives on 43 priests
d: A Suffolk County grand jury report of about 180 pages, presented by District Attorney Thomas Spota in February 2003 after a nine-month investigation, found that at least 58 abusive priests had been protected by the Diocese of Rockville Centre. Officials used sham policies, a bogus 'intervention team' that silenced victims and a 'legal affairs' team that worked to block claims, moved abusers between parishes where they often had access to children, and disregarded advice to give them psychiatric care. The grand jury said the failures could not be attributed to incompetence.

n: Second Philadelphia grand jury — priests still in ministry (2011)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
cover: A senior archdiocesan official was charged with moving priests with abuse complaints to new parishes without warning; up to 37 priests with credible allegations remained in ministry
d: A second Philadelphia grand jury reported in February 2011 that as many as 37 priests remained in active ministry despite credible allegations of sexual abuse. Two priests, a former priest and a Catholic school teacher were charged with raping boys, and Monsignor William Lynn, a former senior archdiocesan official, was charged and accused of transferring problem priests to new parishes without warning anyone of earlier complaints. On 8 March 2011 the archdiocese suspended 21 priests while their cases were reviewed.

n: St. Joseph's Orphanage, Burlington — Vermont task force (2020)
who: St. Joseph's Orphanage, run with roles for the Catholic Diocese of Burlington, the Sisters of Providence and Vermont Catholic Charities
cover: The Attorney General blamed police and prosecutors for not investigating allegations when they were first made; the Sisters of Providence had not produced documents the task force requested by the time the report was finished
d: A task force of the Vermont Attorney General, Burlington's mayor, the Chittenden County State's Attorney, the Vermont State Police and Burlington police investigated former residents' allegations for two years after a 2018 BuzzFeed News report. Its report of about 300 pages, released on 14 December 2020, said 'it is clear abuse happened and children suffered', including physical and sexual abuse, but found too little evidence to prove alleged murders. Attorney General T.J. Donovan said police and prosecutors had failed to investigate complaints when first made; no charges were possible because of time limits.

n: New York Attorney General v. Diocese of Buffalo (2020–2022)
who: Catholic Diocese of Buffalo; retired Bishop Richard Malone and Auxiliary Bishop Edward Grosz
cover: The Attorney General alleged diocesan leaders protected more than two dozen accused priests by not sending their cases to the Vatican
d: In November 2020 the New York Attorney General sued the Diocese of Buffalo and its retired bishops, alleging that they protected more than two dozen priests accused of child sexual abuse. In a settlement filed on 25 October 2022 the diocese accepted enhanced child-protection measures and an independent compliance auditor, and the two bishops were barred from fiduciary roles in New York charities.

n: Rhode Island Attorney General — Diocese of Providence (2026)
who: Catholic Diocese of Providence
cover: The diocese kept abuse secret and failed to report it to civil authorities; under Bishops McVinney and Gelineau accused priests were moved or sent to 'treatment' and returned to ministry, where some abused again; the diocese refused in-person interviews
d: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha published a report on 4 March 2026 after an investigation begun in 2019. It identified 75 credibly accused clergy and more than 300 victims abused between 1950 and 2011. It found the diocese kept abuse secret, did not report it to civil authorities, and under Bishops Russell McVinney and Louis Gelineau moved accused priests or returned them to ministry after 'treatment'. Four current or former priests were charged during the investigation.

n: Ropes & Gray report for the US Olympic Committee — Nassar (2018)
who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics
cover: USA Gymnastics' CEO told the USOC's CEO and chief of sport performance of allegations against Nassar in 2015; neither shared it and the USOC took no action until press reports in September 2016
d: A 233-page report by the law firm Ropes & Gray, commissioned by the US Olympic Committee and released on 10 December 2018, was based on more than 100 interviews over 10 months. It found that in 2015 USA Gymnastics' chief executive told the USOC's chief executive and its chief of sport performance that national team members had alleged abuse by Larry Nassar, and that the USOC took no action from July 2015 until the Indianapolis Star published in September 2016. The USOC fired its chief of sport performance the day the report was released.

n: Indian Health Service — Presidential Task Force after pediatrician Stanley Patrick Weber (2020)
place: Pine Ridge, South Dakota (IHS hospital); also Browning, Montana
who: US Indian Health Service (IHS)
cover: After complaints the IHS transferred Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years; staff did not know their reporting obligations
d: Stanley Patrick Weber, an Indian Health Service pediatrician, was convicted of sexually abusing young boys at IHS hospitals in Montana and South Dakota. A White House task force chaired by US Attorney Trent Shores released a report on 23 July 2020 finding that officials across the agency did not understand their legal duties to report suspected abuse, that the agency sometimes overlooked doctors' troubled work histories to fill posts, and that parts of its child-protection policy conflicted with federal law. After complaints, the agency had moved Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years.

n: Jericho Hill School for the Deaf, Vancouver — Berger special counsel and BC Ombudsman (1992–1993)
who: Jericho Hill Provincial School for the Deaf (BC Ministry of Education)
cover: A boy's 1982 disclosure to a school psychologist was passed to a government social worker, but school authorities stopped the planned investigation; in 1987 police could not gather enough evidence for charges; the province fought a class action through the courts before settling in 2004
d: In 1982 a teenage boy told a psychologist working for the provincial school for deaf children that a counsellor had sexually abused him, but school authorities stopped the planned investigation. More students disclosed abuse in 1987; police could not gather enough evidence for charges, and more than 20 students were found to have abused other students. Former judge Thomas Berger, appointed special counsel in 1992, concluded that the abuse had occurred, and the BC Ombudsman issued Public Report No. 32 on the abuse of deaf students on 8 November 1993. More than 300 former students received payments under a 1992 compensation plan, and in 2004 the province committed $15.6 million to settle a class action.

n: Wood Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service — paedophile inquiry (1997)
who: A Sydney paedophile network linked to convicted sex offender Colin Fisk; a group of NSW police detectives
cover: The network bribed a group of detectives for advance warning of police scrutiny; the Commission was highly critical of how police, prosecutors and public servants handled child sex-offence cases
d: The Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service under Justice James Wood (1994–1997) had its terms widened in 1995 to cover paedophile networks, the care of at-risk minors and police guidelines for investigating sex offences against minors; Volume IV of its final report is the paedophile inquiry. It found a network involving convicted offender Colin Fisk that shared child abuse material, procured under-age sexual partners and invested in an under-age male brothel in Surry Hills, and that it had a corrupt relationship with a group of detectives who sold it advance warning of police scrutiny. The Commission found no compelling evidence for claims of a large ring of prominent professionals protected by senior police.

n: Australian Human Rights Commission — 'Change the Routine', gymnastics review (2021)
who: Gymnastics Australia and the sport of gymnastics in Australia
cover: Complaints of abuse and harm were not adequately addressed and athletes' voices were silenced
d: Gymnastics Australia engaged the Australian Human Rights Commission in August 2020 after repeated abuse claims; the Commission's report 'Change the Routine' was released on 3 May 2021. Drawing on 57 interviews and 138 submissions, it heard of emotional, physical and sexual abuse in a sport whose participants are predominantly young girls, found that complaints were not adequately addressed and that children were not effectively safeguarded, and described a 'win-at-all-costs' culture. It made 12 recommendations, including an apology, which Gymnastics Australia accepted.

n: Poland — Diocese of Sosnowiec independent commission (2026)
who: Catholic Diocese of Sosnowiec
cover: Bishops were repeatedly alerted, including by reliable sources, but often took no action; where they acted, they usually moved the priest to another parish.
d: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed, 96% of them under 15, and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly alerted but in some cases took no action, and accused priests were often transferred rather than punished. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors.

n: France — National Assembly inquiry into failings of sports federations (2024)
who: French sports federations (incl. judo, ice sports, football), sports ministry
cover: The commission described a culture of silence 'at every level', reaching the highest level of the state; the ministry did not give the rapporteur its Signal-sports tracking table, and the data it did provide were 'very incomplete'.
d: A National Assembly commission of inquiry chaired by Béatrice Bellamy, with Sabrina Sebaihi as rapporteur, worked from July 2023 and presented its report in January 2024 after 92 hearings. It found that by November 2023 the ministry's Signal-sports cell had handled over 1,800 reports involving more than 1,200 people, with eight in ten victims minors at the time. Background checks on volunteers, required since 2006, only began working in 2021, and 42 federations were behind. The report described a culture of silence and concealment in federations and in the state.

n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on abuse in sport (2022)
who: German sports clubs and federations (West and East Germany)
d: Germany's federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a case study on sport on 27 September 2022, based on 72 reports from victims and witnesses and three personal accounts. Most abuse happened in organised club sport, especially competitive sport, by mostly male coaches, trainers or teachers in positions of power, and two-thirds of victims were abused repeatedly. Nearly a fifth of reports concerned sport in the GDR. Few cases had been uncovered or dealt with; victims often found their accounts denied, played down or covered up.

n: Germany — Nordelbian Lutheran Church expert commission (Ahrensburg, 2014)
who: Former Nordelbian Evangelical Lutheran Church (now Nordkirche)
cover: The Ahrensburg pastor went unpunished because the offences were time-barred, as were many others; Hamburg bishop Maria Jepsen resigned over the scandal.
d: An independent commission published its final report in October 2014 on sexual abuse in the former Nordelbian Lutheran Church. It examined 14 pastors against whom the church opened 16 disciplinary proceedings between 1993 and 2012, for acts from 1973 to 2011 against children, adolescents and adults. The case that started it was a pastor in Ahrensburg who abused at least a dozen boys and girls over more than 20 years and went unpunished because the acts were time-barred. Hamburg bishop Maria Jepsen resigned over the scandal, and Bishop Kirsten Fehrs called the report shameful and shocking.

n: Germany — Archdiocese of Cologne, Gercke report (2021)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Cologne
cover: The report counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior archdiocesan officials; an earlier report by Westpfahl Spilker Wastl was withheld by the archdiocese.
d: Criminal lawyer Björn Gercke, mandated by the archdiocese, presented an 800-page report on 18 March 2021 covering 1975 to 2018. It found 314 victims, more than half under 14, and 202 accused clergy and lay staff. It counted 75 breaches of duty by eight senior officials, among them the later Archbishop of Hamburg Stefan Heße, while clearing Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki of breach of duty. Woelki had withheld an earlier report by another law firm, which caused a long crisis in the archdiocese.

n: Germany — Diocese of Aachen, Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2020)
who: Catholic Diocese of Aachen
cover: The report assigned personal responsibility to former Bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his vicar general Manfred von Holtum.
d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the diocese, presented its report on 12 November 2020 after reviewing files from 1965 to 2019. It found indications of at least 175 cases of sexual abuse of children and adolescents by 81 clerics (79 priests and two deacons), most victims aged 8 to 14. It assigned personal responsibility to, among others, former bishop Heinrich Mussinghoff and his former vicar general Manfred von Holtum.

n: Germany — Diocese of Osnabrück, University of Osnabrück study (interim report 2022, final report 2024)
who: Catholic Diocese of Osnabrück
cover: The interim report found Bishop Franz-Josef Bode repeatedly left accused priests in office and gave some roles, including youth ministry, that enabled further offences; Bode resigned in March 2023.
d: Historians and lawyers at the University of Osnabrück led by Hans Schulte-Nölke and Siegrid Westphal, commissioned by the diocese, presented a roughly 600-page interim report on 20 September 2022 on sexual violence by clergy since 1945; it criticised the handling of allegations under Bishop Franz-Josef Bode (from 1995) and his predecessors, finding he repeatedly left accused priests in office and assigned some to posts that enabled further abuse. Bode accepted responsibility and resigned in 2023. The final report, presented on 2 October 2024, named 122 accused clerics, about 4% of priests who served in the diocese since 1945 (an area that until 1995 included today's Archdiocese of Hamburg), and 349 identifiable victims with firm indications of at least 60 more; the study says the hidden number may be up to ten times higher.

n: Archdiocese of Paderborn — University of Paderborn study (2026)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Paderborn; archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt
cover: The study found sexual violence against children was concealed over decades; the tenures of Cardinals Jaeger and Degenhardt were assessed critically.
d: Historians at the University of Paderborn, commissioned by the archdiocese, published their study on 12 March 2026. It identified 210 accused people and 489 victims and found that sexual violence against children was concealed for decades under Archbishops Lorenz Jaeger and Johannes Joachim Degenhardt. Paderborn city council then voted to rename streets named after both cardinals and to remove them from its honorary citizens. In September 2026 the archdiocese's independent review commission reported 262 accused clergy and church employees known by the end of June 2026.

n: Diocese of Augsburg — independent review commission study (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Augsburg; bishops and vicars general 1949–2019
cover: Diocesan leaders did not respond appropriately to allegations for decades: share of inappropriate handling 54.5% under Freundorfer, 63.6% under Stimpfle, 68.8% under Dammertz, 33.3% under Mixa, 5.9% under Zdarsa.
d: The diocese's independent review commission (UAKA) presented a 206-page study on 30 October 2025, built on the diocese's MHG-study data covering 1,507 personnel files of diocesan clergy. It found 77 accused linked to 193 offences against 156 victims, about two-thirds male and 42.5% under 14, with offences back to 1948. Diocesan leaders handled allegations inappropriately for decades, in up to 68.8% of cases under one bishop; handling improved after the 2002 guidelines. Bishop Bertram Meier said the diocese bore grave guilt.

n: Archdiocese of Hamburg — University of Ulm study of abuse in Mecklenburg 1946–1989 (2023)
who: Catholic Church in Mecklenburg (Archdiocese of Hamburg); East German Ministry for State Security (Stasi)
cover: The Stasi recruited suspects as informers, so no prosecutions followed; church leaders knew, and church–state arrangements such as moving suspects to West Germany kept cases quiet.
d: Forensic psychiatrists at the University of Ulm led by Manuela Dudeck, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Hamburg, presented their study in Schwerin on 24 February 2023. Reviewing 1,503 church and Stasi files, they identified 19 suspects and 40 victims; the 13 victims interviewed had been about 10 years old on average when the abuse began. Parishes and church leaders knew of abuse, and the study found a culture of silence and partly active cover-up. The Stasi recruited suspects as informers and used them, so prosecutions did not follow, and church–state arrangements such as moves to West Germany kept cases quiet.

n: Franciscan Minorites (German province) — independent study (2024)
who: Order of Friars Minor Conventual (Minorites), German province
cover: Some accused abused for almost 30 years before sanctions took hold; threatened consequences were not enforced across changes of superiors.
d: Lawyers Petra Ladenburger and Martina Lörsch presented a 152-page study on 10 June 2024, the first independent, externally overseen study of a Catholic order in Germany under the 2021 agreement between the orders' conference (DOK) and the federal abuse commissioner. It assessed allegations against nine friars since the 1960s; one friar was accused of abusing 20 people, and many victims were children in the order's boarding schools in Bonn and Würzburg. The committee overseeing the study said some accused abused for nearly 30 years before effective sanctions, because successive superiors did not enforce threatened consequences.

n: Albertinum Gerolstein — Diocese of Trier boarding school report (2022)
who: Diocese of Trier — Bischöfliches Internat Albertinum, Gerolstein; its three priest-directors
cover: The diocese lacked effective oversight; pupils who reported beatings were not believed and survivors received no help.
d: Bettina Janssen and Claudia Bundschuh presented their final report of about 140 pages on the diocesan boarding school Albertinum in Gerolstein on 11 February 2022, covering 1946 until it closed in 1983. Fifty-four former pupils came forward. Violence, mostly physical but including sexualised violence, was part of daily life; all three directors, who were priests, and one lay employee committed sexualised violence. Bishop Stephan Ackermann apologised and admitted the diocese had lacked effective oversight; by February 2023 the diocese had paid more than 650,000 euros to former pupils.

n: Independent Commission (UKASK) study of paedosexual networks in Berlin (2021)
who: Paedosexual networks in Berlin; supporters among scientists, the Greens, child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene; Berlin authorities
cover: Authorities looked away for a long time and held victims partly responsible; in the 1960s–70s foster children were placed with paedosexual men, partly on the advice of educators.
d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse (UKASK) published a preliminary study by Iris Hax and Sven Reiß on 24 February 2021 on paedosexual networks in Berlin from the 1970s to the 2000s. It found that groups of men who sexually exploited boys used social movements and had support from scientists, for a time from the Greens, and from child-rights groups and parts of the left-liberal and autonomist scene, while the women's movement opposed them. Authorities looked away and partly blamed victims; boys were also commercially exploited around Bahnhof Zoo. The commission called for a nationwide investigation of such networks.

n: Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022)
who: Seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol (Martinsbühel, Scharnitz, Josefinum/Volders, Bubenburg/Fügen, St. Josef/Mils, Thurnfeld/Hall, Elisabethinum/Axams); Diocese of Innsbruck; Tyrolean youth welfare
cover: Survivors said the state youth welfare office and school authorities looked too little; church and state officials acknowledged institutional responsibility.
d: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022, written by historians Ina Friedmann and Friedrich Stepanek. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described structural, physical, psychological and sexualised violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister looked after up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Bishop Hermann Glettler called the findings 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions, and the state social affairs councillor apologised.

n: Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone (South Tyrol)
cover: Handling of abuse cases until 2010 was a systemic failure; one priest was removed only in 2010 despite allegations from the 1960s.
d: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its 631-page report on 20 January 2025, described as the first fully independent study of its kind in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven and was removed only in 2010. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a general and highly systemic failure. Bishop Ivo Muser said 'every case is one too many' and that victims' suffering should fill the church with shame.

n: Catalonia — Síndic de Greuges (ombudsman) report on child sexual abuse in the Catholic Church (2020)
who: Catholic religious congregations and dioceses in Catalonia
cover: Congregations generally did not seek out other cases or offer reparation.
d: A commission within the Catalan ombudsman's office (Síndic de Greuges), under Rafael Ribó, published its report on 2 October 2020. Most cases it heard concerned boys aged 5 to 17, abused repeatedly in the 1960s and 1970s on camps and excursions, on church premises and in abusers' flats, with three cases from the 1990s; documents pointed to many more victims than came forward. Religious congregations generally had not looked for other cases or offered reparation. Among seven recommendations, it asked the Catalan Parliament to create an inquiry commission, which the Parliament approved on 27 April 2022.

n: Territorial Abbey of Saint-Maurice — independent working group report (2025)
who: Abbey of Saint-Maurice (canons regular) and its boarding school, Valais
d: An independent working group formed at the request of the abbey, then under a Vatican-appointed apostolic administrator, by Neuchâtel attorney general Pierre Aubert presented its findings on 20 June 2025. Historians of the University of Fribourg (Anne-Françoise Praz, Stéphanie Roulin and others) and retired judge Claire-Lise Mayor Aubert heard about 50 witnesses and 24 clergy and examined sexual violence at the abbey and its boarding school from 1960 to 2024. They found sexualised touching by canons, ambiguous photo sessions, exhibitionism and use of child abuse material; since 1970 five criminal penalty orders had been issued against three canons and a novice, and members with ambiguous or unlawful conduct were left in office without precautions. The mandate did not cover the abbey's collège.

n: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false
who: Saeima investigation commission chaired by MP Jānis Ādamsons; former PM Andris Šķēle, ex-justice minister Valdis Birkavs, State Revenue Service head Andrejs Sončiks (accused, cleared)
d: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who on 17 February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission about them was false. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander; in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats. None of the officials was charged.

n: Amsterdam daycare abuse case (Het Hofnarretje) and the Gunning commission
who: Robert Mikelsons (childcare worker at Het Hofnarretje and Jenno's Knuffelparadijs) and his partner Richard van O.
cover: An anonymous tip to Meld Misdaad Anoniem in 2008 was not acted on; the Gunning commission called it a missed opportunity.
d: Childcare worker Robert Mikelsons abused babies and toddlers at two Amsterdam daycare centres and as a babysitter between February 2007 and January 2010. On 21 May 2012 the Amsterdam district court sentenced him to 18 years plus compulsory psychiatric detention (TBS); he was charged over 67 children and admitted abusing 87, and the appeal court raised the sentence to 19 years on 26 April 2013. His partner Richard van O. was sentenced to six years as an accessory. On 15 April 2011 a commission chaired by Louise Gunning-Schepers found that daycare centres, government bodies and others had failed, that risk signals were missed, and that a 2008 anonymous report had not been acted on.

n: Queensland — Crime and Misconduct Commission inquiry into abuse of children in foster care, 'Protecting children' (2004)
who: Queensland Department of Families; foster care and child protection system
d: In late May 2003 a woman told a Department of Families office that she had been sexually abused for 13 years in foster care by a family member who was an approved foster carer and by visitors to the household, and that other children placed with the family were also abused. In July 2003 the Premier referred concerns about the foster care system to the Crime and Misconduct Commission, which audited abuse notifications against current carers and held public hearings from 13 October 2003. Its report, released in January 2004, found the department's response 'completely inadequate' at most of nine points where children could have been protected, and concluded that the child protection system had failed Queensland children. It made 110 recommendations, including creating a separate Department of Child Safety and a Child Guardian.

n: Charity Commission statutory inquiry — Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain (Jehovah's Witnesses), 2014–2023
place: Mill Hill, London (Watch Tower Britain headquarters during the inquiry)
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain; Jehovah's Witness congregations in Britain (now under the Kingdom Hall Trust)
cover: Commission found trustees were not as straightforward or transparent as they should have been about who held safeguarding responsibility; repeated legal challenges 'substantially constrained' the inquiry (insufficient evidence of deliberate obstruction)
d: The Charity Commission for England and Wales opened a statutory inquiry into the national Jehovah's Witness charity in May 2014 over its safeguarding policy, after a 2007 inquiry into a London congregation found it had no child protection policy and the NSPCC found in 2013 that the national policy conflicted with UK law and guidance. Watch Tower challenged the inquiry in the courts; the Supreme Court refused it permission to appeal in December 2016, and a tribunal judge said its delays created 'ongoing risks' to children. The Commission's report of 4 August 2023 closed the inquiry because responsibility for safeguarding in more than 1,000 congregations had passed to the Kingdom Hall Trust, which it placed under a compliance case. Jehovah's Witness organisations had reported 67 allegations of child sexual abuse against 67 people for 2009–2019 to IICSA.

n: IICSA — the internet and child sexual abuse (2020)
who: Online platforms and services (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat named); UK government and law enforcement
d: IICSA's report on the internet, published 12 March 2020, found that millions of indecent images of children are in circulation and that most are on mainstream platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat, not only the dark web. It cited BT data of more than 30,000 attempts every 24 hours to view abuse material, and an NSPCC estimate that about 500,000 men in the UK had viewed such images. It recommended pre-screening of uploads, stricter age verification and international action to remove images hosted abroad.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — child migrants sent from Scotland (Case Study 8)
who: Charities, religious orders and governments that ran child migration schemes from Scotland to Canada and Australia
d: Lady Smith published the first volume of findings on child migration on 21 March 2023 and a second volume in September 2023. She found that many thousands of children were sent from Scotland, mainly to Canada and later Australia, and that some were sexually abused at their destinations, including by men in holy orders and by members of a paedophile ring. About 80,000 children were sent from the UK to Canada by 1920 and about 7,000 to Australia between 1912 and 1970; 45 people gave evidence.

n: Scotland — Shaw historical abuse systemic review (residential care 1950–1995)
