who: Residential schools and children's homes in Scotland (e.g. Nazareth House Kilmarnock, Quarriers Village); successive governments and local authorities
d: Tom Shaw, former chief inspector of education in Northern Ireland, reviewed for the Scottish Executive the laws, rules and records governing residential schools and children's homes from 1950 to 1995; his report was published in November 2007. He found the regulations were 'extensive and in many respects impressive' but that successive governments and authorities failed to make sure they were followed, and that abuse would likely have been less common had they been honoured. About 35 former residents were interviewed and about 80 other people gave evidence. He recommended a national task group, a centre for former residents and new law on children's home records.

n: Northern Ireland — Marshall independent inquiry into child sexual exploitation (2014)
who: Individuals and groups exploiting children in Northern Ireland, some using purported paramilitary links; children in residential care
d: Health minister Edwin Poots commissioned Professor Kathleen Marshall after the PSNI said in September 2013 it was investigating the suspected exploitation of 22 young people. Her report, published 18 November 2014, identified 100 to 145 children at significant risk of sexual exploitation and said the real number was likely much higher. It found individuals with purported paramilitary links used fear to exploit young people, but no targeting by paramilitary groups as such, and no evidence of cover-up. It made 17 key recommendations.

n: Leicestershire children's homes — Frank Beck and the Kirkwood Inquiry
place: Leicestershire (The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road, The Beeches)
who: Leicestershire County Council Social Services; officer-in-charge Frank Beck
d: Frank Beck ran three Leicestershire council children's homes, The Poplars, Ratcliffe Road and The Beeches, between 1973 and 1986, and resigned in March 1986 after two male residential social workers complained of sexual advances. On 29 November 1991 he received five life sentences for assaults on more than 100 children; police took statements from nearly 400 children. The Leicestershire inquiry chaired by Andrew Kirkwood QC, reported in 1993, was strongly critical of the management of the county's social services, finding that early warnings were ignored, supervision was absent and complaints were poorly investigated. Its hearings were held in private.

n: Savile in schools and children's homes — 14 investigations with independent oversight (2015)
who: 14 councils, charities and schools (incl. Barnardo's, Action for Children, Henshaws Society for Blind People, Sevenoaks School) named in information about Jimmy Savile
d: After Michael Gove's statement of 27 March 2014, 14 investigations were carried out by councils, institutions and successor organisations into information linking Jimmy Savile to their children's homes and schools in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. The Department for Education statement of 26 February 2015 reported that none reached firm conclusions: many informants were judged credible, but there was not enough corroborating evidence for definite findings. Lucy Scott-Moncrieff's independent oversight found the investigations had been conducted in an appropriate and robust fashion.

n: Rotherham — Casey inspection of the council (2015)
who: Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council
cover: Inspectors found the council went to 'some lengths' to cover up information and silence whistleblowers, and used severance payments and compromise agreements instead of holding staff to account.
d: Louise Casey's government-ordered inspection, published 4 February 2015, judged Rotherham council 'not fit for purpose' and in denial about continuing failures after the Jay report. It found the council still treated child sexual exploitation as a social care issue, could not assure the public that taxi licence holders were fit and proper (86% of audited complaint investigations were inadequate), and had covered up information and silenced whistleblowers. The council leader and cabinet resigned and the government sent in commissioners.

n: Isle of Man — Knottfield children's home (Tynwald committee report)
who: Knottfield children's home (Isle of Man Government); house parent Joseph Marshall
d: A Tynwald scrutiny committee (Social Affairs Policy Review Committee) chaired by David Cretney reported on 6 October 2018 on the 'horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse' by Joseph Marshall while he ran Knottfield children's home with his wife between 1973 and 1983, and made 11 recommendations. Marshall had been convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield in 1992 and was jailed for six years in April 2022 for sexually abusing two boys there. The report was withdrawn during the criminal case; the Isle of Man Government apologised on 16 January 2023 for mistakes that contributed to the abuse and supported all 11 recommendations.

n: Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review
place: Dublin (St Patrick's Guild; Tusla; Adoption Authority of Ireland)
who: St Patrick's Guild adoption society; Tusla and the Adoption Authority of Ireland (record holders); the Irish state
d: In May 2018 the Irish government announced that 126 people placed through the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been illegally registered as the birth children of their adoptive parents. An independent review then sampled 1,496 of about 150,000 adoption records; its report, published in March 2021, found about 265 files with suspicious markers and estimated 5,540 to 19,980 files might show similar signs. Tusla reported evidence of coerced consent, children placed abroad with little documentation and altered names and birth dates; the report did not recommend a full file review.

n: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cover: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.
d: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.

n: Paraguay — Truth and Justice Commission: sexual slavery of girls by senior officers of the Stroessner regime
who: Senior military and police officers of the Stroessner regime; procurers who took girls from their families
d: Paraguay's Comisión de Verdad y Justicia, created by law in October 2003, presented its final report on 28 August 2008 after collecting more than 2,000 testimonies on the 1954–1989 dictatorship. Its conclusions state that sexual violence against women and girls was fostered by the repressive apparatus and reached its extreme in 'sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime', and that young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts at the service of officers. It recorded that 10.8% of victims were minors at the time and noted large under-reporting of sexual violence. Amnesty International reported that girls as young as seven were believed to have been taken from their homes for senior military officers.

n: Turkey — parliamentary research commission on child abuse after the Ensar Foundation dormitory case (2016)
place: Ankara (Grand National Assembly); triggered by Karaman
who: Student houses in Karaman linked to the Ensar Foundation; student dormitories nationally
d: On 24 March 2016 the Turkish Grand National Assembly unanimously set up a research commission on child abuse after a teacher in Karaman was arrested for abusing 10 children in student houses, two of them owned by the Ensar Foundation. It began work on 28 April; by July its only field visit had been to Karaman, where the provincial family directorate gave members a report that blamed the victims' families. Its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, a permanent children's rights committee in parliament, a child-protection coordination centre, background checks for people working with children and a wider penal definition of sexual abuse. Opposition (CHP) members said the report was general and theoretical and that the commission had not visited state nurseries, prisons or Syrian camps.

n: Brazil — Chamber of Deputies inquiry asks indictment of 37, including a mayor and state deputies (2014)
who: Local politicians and others in Amazonas, Minas Gerais and other states
d: A parliamentary inquiry of the Chamber of Deputies, installed in 2012 with Deputy Liliam Sá as rapporteur, approved its final report on 4 June 2014. It asked for the indictment of 37 people for sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, among them the mayor of Coari (Amazonas), Adail Pinheiro, a serving Amazonas state deputy, a former state deputy and a former president of the Três Corações city council.

n: Ecuador — National Assembly 'AAMPETRA' commission on sexual violence in schools (2018)
who: Teachers and staff of public and private schools; Ministry of Education
cover: Commission found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities
d: Ecuador's National Assembly set up a multiparty occasional commission in 2017 after families of pupils abused at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari (AAMPETRA) in Quito, where 41 children were abused, mobilised. It reviewed cases from 2013 to 2017 and, in a report approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities and concluded that former ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch's later analysis of government data counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.

n: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004)
who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF), Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Civil Defence Forces (CDF), Sierra Leone Army, West Side Boys
d: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone released its final report in October 2004. It found that the RUF and the AFRC 'deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years', using them as sexual and domestic slaves and 'wives'; in a few cases the children were below ten. It also found that the CDF carried out a deliberate strategy of rape, sexual slavery and other sexual violations against girls, and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex. Of 189 allegations of sexual slavery of women and girls reported to it, 72.5% were attributed to the RUF and 11.6% to the AFRC.

n: DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003)
who: All parties: FAC (later FARDC), RCD-G, MLC, RCD-K/ML, RCD-N, UPC and PUSIC, FNI and FRPI, FAPC, Mayi-Mayi, ex-FAR/Interahamwe and others
d: The UN human rights office's Mapping Exercise report, published on 1 October 2010, covered the most serious violations in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described 'the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault allegedly by all combatant forces' against women and girls, including Hutu refugee children in 1996–97, and the widespread use of child soldiers by all parties, who suffered murder, rape and torture in military camps. It listed 12 parties named by the Secretary-General for recruiting children, among them the national army.

n: Afghanistan — Human Rights Commission national inquiry into bacha bazi (2014)
who: Powerful men who keep boys for dancing and sexual abuse
cover: The Commission's chair said the law did not properly prevent the practice and called for an end to the 'culture of impunity'
d: The Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission concluded a national inquiry into the causes and consequences of bacha bazi, the sexual abuse of boys kept by powerful men to dance, in August 2014. It held 71 focus groups and 17 public hearings in 17 provinces, attended by almost 2,200 people, and two-thirds of victims said they received money from the perpetrators. Its chair, Sima Samar, said the practice was a crime that the law did not properly prevent and called on the government to fight the culture of impunity.

n: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
place: DR Congo (MONUSCO, 44 allegations) and other UN missions; report issued at UN Headquarters, New York
who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cover: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action
d: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.

n: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
d: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

n: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cover: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.
d: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.

n: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
d: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

n: Scale of Harm — prevalence of livestreamed abuse in the Philippines (IJM / Rights Lab)
who: Family members and neighbours paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse
d: IJM and the University of Nottingham Rights Lab estimated the prevalence of trafficking to produce child sexual exploitation material in the Philippines. IJM states that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, that the median victim age in its earlier 2020 study was 11, average abuse lasted two years, and 9% of victims were 3 or younger. IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries.

n: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
d: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

n: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
d: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

n: NCMEC: 6.9 million fewer Facebook reports after Messenger encryption
who: Meta (Facebook Messenger default end-to-end encryption)
d: NCMEC reported that CyberTipline reports fell from 36.2 million in 2023 to 20.5 million in 2024 (29.2 million incidents after adjusting for 'bundling'). It attributed part of the fall to Meta's default end-to-end encryption in Facebook Messenger (December 2023 to summer 2024), with 6.9 million fewer reports from Facebook, and to Google, X, Discord, Microsoft and Synchronoss reporting 20% fewer. NCMEC says the drop came even though the 2024 REPORT Act added mandatory reporting of enticement and child sex trafficking.

n: US Kids Online Safety Act, EARN IT Act and REPORT Act
who: US Congress
d: The EARN IT Act, which would condition platforms' liability shield on child-safety practices, was introduced in 2020, 2022 and 2023 and died in committee. The Kids Online Safety Act passed the Senate 91–3 on 30 July 2024 but did not pass the House that Congress; it was reintroduced in May 2025, and in June 2026 the House Energy and Commerce Committee reportedly agreed a revised version. The REPORT Act, passed in 2024, expanded platforms' mandatory reporting to NCMEC to include online enticement and child sex trafficking and raised fines for failing to report; NCMEC attributed a jump in child sex trafficking reports, from 5,976 in the first half of 2024 to 62,891 in the first half of 2025, to the law. The TAKE IT DOWN Act was signed in May 2025.

n: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
d: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

n: LS Models / 'Alex Model' raids, Ukraine
who: 'Alex Model' agency (LS-Models brands)
cover: Despite surveillance and arrests the legal outcome was described as lenient.
d: A Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through TV, newspaper and radio adverts and produced sexualised images sold worldwide under 'LS' brands from 2001. Police raided it in July 2004; at the same time over 150 people were arrested in Australia for possession and distribution.

n: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
d: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

n: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
d: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

n: Tbilisi photo studio producing abuse material for foreign buyers
who: Photo studio owners and foreign clients
d: Georgian police, with Australian and US authorities and Europol, arrested 11 members of a group including studio owners and American and Australian citizens who arranged the production of sexual images of girls aged 8 to 14 in rented apartments in Tbilisi. Some girls were abused with parental consent in exchange for 500–3,000 GEL (about €150–900).

n: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
d: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.

n: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
d: Danish National Police, acting on information from Save the Children about images found online, arrested a man and his wife who had posted images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter; from November 2001 the US Customs CyberSmuggling Center coordinated US inquiries with Danish police, INTERPOL and NCMEC. On 9 August 2002 US Customs announced 10 arrests of US citizens, with 10 more suspects arrested in Denmark, Belgium, Germany, England, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and 45 children rescued, 37 of them in the US; in many cases parents were abusing their own children. Fifteen suspects, five of them foreign nationals, were indicted on federal conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of California on 8 August 2002.

n: NCMEC 2025: generative AI in 1.5 million reports
who: NCMEC CyberTipline
d: NCMEC's first look at 2025 data: over 1.5 million reports had a generative-AI connection, 1.1 million of them from Amazon AI Services with no actionable information. Excluding those: 12,000+ involved CSAM in AI training data, 7,000+ users generating or possessing AI CSAM, 30,000+ attempts to generate CSAM from uploaded images, 145,000+ altering CSAM files. NCMEC says more than 275 victims of AI-generated CSAM have been identified since 2023.

n: Rotherham — Jay inquiry (1,400 children, 1997–2013)
who: Group-based exploitation networks; Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council; South Yorkshire Police
cover: Three earlier reports (2002, 2003, 2013) on exploitation were effectively suppressed or ignored; police did not treat the abuse as a priority.
d: Professor Alexis Jay's independent inquiry, published 26 August 2014, estimated that about 1,400 children were sexually exploited in Rotherham between 1997 and 2013, some as young as 11. It described the collective failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police as 'blatant'. The report said most known perpetrators were of Pakistani heritage, and that frontline staff were confused about what might be seen as racist. The council leader resigned within hours of publication.

n: Telford — Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation
who: Group-based exploitation networks; West Mercia Police; Telford & Wrekin Council
cover: Concerns raised by officers, youth workers and teachers in the 1990s were not taken seriously; specialist CSE teams were cut to near zero after Operation Chalice.
d: The inquiry chaired by Tom Crowther QC, published 12 July 2022, found more than 1,000 children were sexually exploited in Telford over at least 30 years. Agencies dismissed the abuse as 'child prostitution', blamed children for 'lifestyle choices', and failed to investigate partly from nervousness about race. Seven men were jailed in 2013 after Operation Chalice. West Mercia Police and the council apologised; the inquiry found no evidence of corruption.

n: Halifax/Calderdale — West Yorkshire grooming trials
who: Grooming networks; West Yorkshire Police
d: On 6 November 2024, 20 men were jailed for more than 200 years combined for raping and abusing four girls aged 12 to 16 in Calderdale between 2001 and 2010, after three West Yorkshire Police investigations. In May 2026 six more men were convicted over the abuse of one girl from 2006 to 2009, which she reported to police in 2019.

n: Home Office paper on group-based CSE characteristics (2020)
who: Home Office
d: The Home Office paper published 15 December 2020 reviewed the evidence on group-based child sexual exploitation. It said research found group-based offenders were 'most commonly White' and that available data did not support conclusions that any one ethnic group was over-represented, while stressing that data were poor and inconsistently recorded. The Home Secretary's foreword said community and cultural factors were 'clearly relevant'. The 2025 Casey audit later said such flawed data had been used to dismiss concerns.

n: Pornhub/MindGeek (Aylo) — card cut-off, DOJ agreement and FTC/Utah settlement
place: Brooklyn, New York (EDNY); Salt Lake City (FTC/Utah)
who: Aylo Holdings (formerly MindGeek), owner of Pornhub
d: After a New York Times column by Nicholas Kristof on 4 December 2020 reported child sexual abuse material and non-consensual videos on Pornhub, the site banned uploads from unverified users and Mastercard (10 Dec 2020) and Visa stopped card acceptance. On 21 December 2023 Aylo entered a deferred prosecution agreement in Brooklyn over unlawful monetary transactions involving sex-trafficking proceeds (linked to GirlsDoPorn, whose victims were adult women), paying over $1.8 million plus victim compensation and accepting a three-year monitor; Aylo did not plead guilty. On 3 September 2025 Aylo agreed to pay $5 million to the FTC and Utah, which alleged it knowingly profited from child sexual abuse material and that its fingerprinting system was ineffective from at least 2017 to August 2021.

n: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
cover: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.
d: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)

n: Philippines blacklists Australian sex offender after AFP warning (2013)
who: Philippine Bureau of Immigration; Australian Federal Police
d: In April 2013 Philippine immigration officers at Manila airport intercepted and blacklisted an Australian convicted in Perth in 2010 of indecent assault on children, travelling on a New Zealand passport and planning to stay in Iloilo, after an Australian police warning that he posed a risk to Filipino children. It is an example of offender travel notifications between countries.

n: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
d: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

n: Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025)
who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
cover: The report says official complicity, including at senior levels, inhibited effective law enforcement.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.

n: Kenya coast — UNICEF/Government study on child sex tourism (2006)
who: Tourists and local clients in Kenya's beach resorts
d: On 19 December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs launched a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 per cent of 12–18-year-old girls living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex; 38 per cent of clients were Kenyan and 44 per cent Italian, German or Swiss tourists. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and acknowledged police and community failure to enforce the law.

n: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
who: Daniel Galván Viña
cover: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.
d: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.

n: Malawi — Dzaleka refugee camp girls recruited for sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
who: Transnational crime syndicates operating from bars and compounds in the camp
cover: The report says official complicity continued to impede enforcement.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says organized transnational syndicates operating from informal bars and housing in Dzaleka camp (about 53,000 refugees in a space for 10,000) recruit girls for sex trafficking inside the camp and in roadside bars along the highway to Lilongwe; the camp is a waypoint on the 'Southern Route' to South Africa. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre.

n: Côte d'Ivoire — girls brought to Abidjan for domestic servitude; Nigerian girls at mines (US TIP 2025)
who: Relatives and Nigerian trafficking networks
d: The 2025 US TIP report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan for school or training and then exploit them in domestic servitude, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; Ivorian women and girls are sex-trafficked especially in Abidjan; and Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls for shop jobs then exploit them in gold-mining and cocoa regions.

n: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
d: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

n: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cover: HRW said Myanmar and Chinese authorities were 'looking away'; police on both sides gave traffickers little reason to fear enforcement.
d: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. One survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. The 2025 US TIP report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.

n: Patong, Phuket — foreign bar owner sentenced to 1,073 years after raid freed six minors (2024)
who: Illegal bar on Bangla Road
cover: Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid; the foreign owner initially fled to a neighbouring country.
d: A 2023 raid on an illegal bar on Bangla Road, Patong, rescued six victims of child sexual exploitation under 18. On 19 July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven defendants, Thai and foreign; the prime defendant, a foreign owner, received a total of 1,073 years. Five senior Patong police were transferred after the raid. The 2025 US TIP report says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sex-trafficked in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels.

n: Japan — 'JK business' and compensated dating (police survey 2024; US TIP 2025)
who: JK businesses, often with organized-crime ties
d: The 'JK business' sells simulated dates and services with high-school girls. A National Police Agency survey at the end of December 2024 counted 91 establishments advertising in this way, 70 per cent in Tokyo. Kanagawa first regulated it in 2011 and Tokyo enacted a dedicated ordinance in 2017. The 2025 US TIP report says JK variants and 'compensated dating', often tied to organized crime, continue to facilitate sex trafficking of Japanese children and of children from China, South Korea, Laos, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.

n: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan — girls lured to cities; children in institutions (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers recruiting via social media
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers lure girls and women from rural Kazakhstan and neighbouring Central Asian, East Asian and Eastern European countries with job offers as waitresses, models or nannies in large cities, and exploit Kazakh women and girls in Russia, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Europe, East Asia and the US. In Uzbekistan, children in institutions are vulnerable to sex trafficking.

n: Sosúa — 29 trafficking victims including 20 minors freed in US–Dominican sting (2015)
who: Local pimping ring in a tourist town
d: In April 2015 Dominican authorities, with HSI Santo Domingo and two private US organisations, lured alleged traffickers to a staged 'sex party' in the tourist town of Sosúa, freeing 29 victims including 20 minors aged 14–17 and arresting seven Dominican nationals (two women, five men), who faced up to 15 years. The 2025 US TIP report says teenage girls are frequently exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and NGOs link rising child victim numbers to weak regulation of tourism.

n: Brazil — child sex tourism in northeastern coastal cities (Fortaleza, Natal, Recife, Salvador)
who: Taxi drivers, hotel and bar staff facilitating foreign offenders
cover: US TIP 2025: no investigations of complicit officials reported; a 2016 child sex-trafficking case involving an elected official in Paraná unresolved.
d: In 2006 Brazil's Federal Police described sex tourism as most frequent in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal, and ran periodic raids, e.g. on a Ponta Negra (Natal) nightclub with 110 foreigners (no children found that night). The 2025 US TIP report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal tourist destinations facilitate child sex trafficking, and cites a study suggesting up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14–17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation.

n: Jamaica — child sex trafficking in resort towns; 6.3% of 12–17-year-olds (US TIP 2025)
who: Family members, 'dons', foreign and local buyers
cover: Endemic corruption and official complicity, including within law enforcement, remained significant concerns.
d: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 prevalence study estimating 6.3 per cent of Jamaican children aged 12–17 had experienced conditions indicative of trafficking. Children are subjected to sex trafficking in resort areas frequented by tourists, sometimes with parental involvement, and men pay girls or their families for sex in some communities.

n: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
d: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

n: Moldova — children recruited online; institution leavers at risk (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers using social media and fake job ads
cover: A former police officer was convicted of labour trafficking (20 years); corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers increasingly use social media and video chat to recruit children through fake job ads and exploit them in commercial sex, use abuse material as a grooming method, and target children in or leaving state institutions. Courts convicted 33 traffickers (22 for sex trafficking) in 2024.

n: France — 10,000–15,000 French teenagers in child sex trafficking (NGO estimate, US TIP 2025)
who: Small networks of young French men using romance schemes
d: The 2025 US TIP report cites NGO estimates that 10,000 to 15,000 French teenagers are victims of child sex trafficking, says authorities estimate more than half of all trafficking victims in France are French girls and young women exploited by small 'romance' networks, and that traffickers recruit girls in government-funded shelters. Criminal networks force children, mostly from Romania and North Africa, to commit crimes.

n: Iraq — officials allegedly coerce ISIS-affiliated families, including children, into sex (US TIP 2025)
who: Security and military officials (alleged, per an international organization); criminal gangs
cover: An international organization reported in 2024 that officials coerce family members of detained children into sex acts in exchange for security clearances or civil documents; the government reported no action on official complicity.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls in IDP camps whose relatives have alleged ISIS ties may face sexual exploitation and sex trafficking by security and military officials, and that some officials allegedly exploit such families, including children, in exchange for documents. Criminal gangs reportedly exploit Syrian women and girls at pilgrimage sites, and Yezidi survivors remain at risk of re-trafficking.

n: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera — Puebla diocese priest in Los Angeles
who: Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Diocese of Tehuacán (Mexico)
cover: Plaintiffs' attorneys produced a 1988 letter from the Bishop of Tehuacán saying he had warned Cardinal Mahony in 1987 about the priest; the archdiocese denied receiving the warning. The priest fled to Mexico after being relieved of duties and was never arrested.
d: A visiting Mexican priest was assigned to two Los Angeles parishes in 1987. A 1988 police report says he abused 26 grade-school children between March 1987 and January 1988, many recruited as altar servers. A parent reported abuse to a pastor on 8 January 1988; he was removed the next day, charged with 19 felony counts of lewd acts on a child, but fled to Mexico before arrest. As of 2004 the case remained open.

n: Ecuador — 103 complaints of sexual violence against clergy (Ecuavisa)
who: Catholic clergy in Ecuador
cover: Victims' families said the church hierarchy refused to share information or file complaints with prosecutors itself, contrary to a National Assembly commission report on sexual violence against children in education.
d: A months-long investigation by Ecuavisa's Visión 360 counted 103 complaints of sexual abuse involving Ecuadorian clergy, with cases in Guayas, Pichincha, Azuay and Los Ríos, including those of Fr César Cordero and Fr Luis Intriago. A survivors' association demanded that such crimes be made imprescriptible, as approved in a referendum.

n: Japan — Bishops' Conference survey: 16 cases
who: Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan (16 dioceses)
cover: Eight accused clerics were transferred; some punished clerics kept working or moved to another diocese; five remained priests. Only one denied case was examined by a third-party panel.
d: The Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan began a survey of all 16 dioceses in May 2019 and published it on 7 April 2020. It found 16 cases of sexual abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s, called 'the tip of the iceberg'. Most victims took 10 to 30 years to report, some 50 to 70 years. Of the accused, seven were Japanese priests and eight religious or missionaries, seven of them foreign. Earlier internal surveys (2002, 2012) had found two and five cases.

n: Royal Commission Case Study 36 — Church of England Boys' Society
place: Tasmania, Adelaide, Brisbane and Sydney dioceses
who: Church of England Boys' Society (now Anglican Boys' Society / Boys' Ministry Australia); Anglican dioceses of Sydney, Brisbane, Adelaide and Tasmania
cover: Allegations were not reported to police at all or not in time; a parish priest told one victim to 'let sleeping dogs lie'. The report found Peter Hollingworth, former Archbishop of Brisbane and later Governor-General, made 'a serious error of judgment' in letting an accused priest continue in ministry.
d: The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse reported in February 2017 that the CEBS youth group gave paedophiles easy access to boys from the 1970s to the 1990s, with abuse on camps, sailing and fishing trips and overnight stays at rectories. It found 'networks of sexual perpetrators at CEBS who had knowledge of each other's sexual offending against boys and in some instances facilitated' it; several associated men were later convicted. It found a focus on protecting the reputation of the church, dioceses, CEBS and clergy.

n: Brazil — three Arapiraca priests convicted (Penedo diocese)
who: Diocese of Penedo
cover: According to the victims, Bishop Valério Breda knew what was happening; he suspended the priests two days after the scandal broke. The convicted priests were not jailed pending appeal.
d: On 19 December 2011 a juvenile court judge in Arapiraca convicted Monsignor Luiz Marques Barbosa (21 years), Monsignor Raimundo Gomes and Fr Edílson Duarte (16 years 4 months each) of abusing altar boys. The case began with complaints from former altar boys in March 2010 and a secretly filmed video broadcast on SBT television.

n: Myanmar — Pathein monastery: four schoolgirls raped
place: Saitta Thuka monastery, Yetho village near Pathein, Ayeyarwady
who: Saitta Thuka monastery (Theravada Buddhist monastic boarding)
cover: The monk disappeared when parents went to police; TIME found police unable or unwilling to say whether a search continued, and described near-blanket immunity for monks, with police deferring to the religious affairs ministry and the Sangha. An ex-monk who reprimanded him was told to move away.
d: Four girls aged 10 to 14 staying free at a monastery so they could attend school were repeatedly raped from June 2017 by the monastery's administrator monk, according to the children and families interviewed by Myanmar Now. The abuse came to light in February 2018; police issued orders to arrest him on sight across several regions. TIME reported up to 300,000 children may live in Myanmar monasteries, with few records kept.

n: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cover: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action
d: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.

n: Archdiocese of Boston — Spotlight 2002 and Massachusetts AG report 2003
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Boston; Cardinal Bernard Law
cover: Accused priests reassigned with Cardinal Law's personal involvement; church alerted law enforcement only twice in six decades; bishops sought leniency for priests and withheld information from prosecutors
d: After the Boston Globe Spotlight series beginning January 2002, Cardinal Law resigned in December 2002. The Massachusetts Attorney General's report of 23 July 2003 found at least 237 priests and 13 other church workers accused of abusing at least 789 minors over six decades, and 'overwhelming evidence' that Law knew and took part in reassigning abusers. No criminal statute allowed charging church leaders.

n: Maryland Attorney General — Archdiocese of Baltimore
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Baltimore
cover: Archdiocese often failed to report to authorities or remove abusers; some accused allowed to retire with support; post-2002 public list omitted known abusers
d: The Maryland Attorney General's report, released in redacted form on 5 April 2023, identified 156 priests and others associated with the Archdiocese of Baltimore who abused more than 600 children over 80 years. Attorney General Anthony Brown described 'repeated coverup' by the church. A judge ordered the names and titles of 37 people redacted.

n: Winter Commission — Archdiocese of St. John's
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. John's; Archbishop Alphonsus Penney
cover: Report assigned Archbishop Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse
d: Archbishop Alphonsus Penney commissioned former Lieutenant Governor Gordon Winter in May 1989 to inquire into sexual abuse of children by clergy of the archdiocese. The 1990 report assigned Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse, and he resigned after its release.

n: IICSA — Roman Catholic Church in England and Wales
who: Catholic Church in England and Wales; Cardinal Vincent Nichols
cover: Accused priests reassigned to other parishes; Holy See and Apostolic Nuncio refused to provide a witness statement
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 10 November 2020 that the Church in England and Wales received more than 900 complaints involving over 3,000 instances of child sexual abuse between 1970 and 2015, with more than 100 allegations a year since 2016. It found the church put its reputation before children and criticised Cardinal Nichols. The Holy See declined to provide a witness statement.

n: Adriaenssens commission and Vangheluwe resignation, Belgium
who: Catholic Church in Belgium, about 29 religious orders; Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges
cover: Judicial raid in June 2010 seized the commission's files (later ruled disproportionate); commission members resigned
d: Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in April 2010 after admitting he abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. The church-backed commission led by psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months; its report of 10 September 2010 recorded 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse and 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files (Operation Chalice/Kelk); an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate.

n: Regensburger Domspatzen choir — Weber report
who: Regensburger Domspatzen cathedral choir and boarding schools, Diocese of Regensburg
cover: Report faulted choir director Georg Ratzinger for 'looking away' and said former bishop Gerhard Ludwig Müller bore 'clear responsibility' for weaknesses in investigating
d: Lawyer Ulrich Weber's final report of 18 July 2017 found that 547 boys at the cathedral choir's schools were, 'with a high degree of plausibility', victims of physical or sexual abuse or both between 1945 and 1992: about 500 cases of physical violence and 67 of sexual violence, by 49 people in all. Violence was worst at the choir's preparatory school. The report faulted Georg Ratzinger, choir director 1964–1994, for 'looking away' and failing to intervene; he said he knew of physical abuse but not sexual abuse.

n: Bernard Preynat and Cardinal Barbarin, Lyon
who: Archdiocese of Lyon; Fr Bernard Preynat; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin
cover: Cardinal Barbarin convicted in March 2019 of failing to report abuse (suspended six months), cleared on appeal and by France's highest court in April 2021
d: Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts between 1971 and 1991; many cases were time-barred and he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991. A church tribunal found him guilty and removed him from the priesthood (announced 4 July 2019), and on 16 March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison. Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted in March 2019 of not reporting him and given a six-month suspended sentence; an appeal court acquitted him in January 2020 and the Cour de cassation upheld that in April 2021. Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 6 March 2020.

n: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
cover: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula
d: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.

n: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
who: Marist Brothers in Chile
cover: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru
d: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.

n: Venezuela — priests accused or convicted 2001–2022
who: Catholic Church in Venezuela
cover: Three of the priests served little or no sentence and returned to ministry
d: A 2022 Washington Post investigation found at least 10 Catholic priests accused or convicted of sexual abuse in Venezuela between 2001 and 2022, with complaints in at least eleven states. Three served little or no sentence and returned to the priesthood. The church confirmed the report's accuracy and announced an investigation.

n: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
d: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

n: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cover: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic
d: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.

n: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland — review 2020
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (with Scout Association of Ireland), now Scouting Ireland
cover: Organisations shielded known or suspected abusers after abuse was reported
d: A review published in May 2020 found that over several decades before their 2004 merger into Scouting Ireland, the Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and the Scout Association of Ireland shielded 275 known or suspected abusers. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Marist and Christian Brothers schools
who: Marist Brothers (St Joseph's College Dumfries, St Columba's College Largs); Christian Brothers (St Ninian's, Falkland)
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on the Christian Brothers, published on 17 February 2021, concluded that the regime at St Ninian's Residential Care Home, Falkland, exposed children to risks of sexual, physical and psychological danger, and that between 1953 and 1983 those risks materialised for many children; 42 witnesses gave evidence. The inquiry also examined the Marist Brothers' St Joseph's College, Dumfries and St Columba's College, Largs, with findings published later in 2021. Two Brothers were jailed in 2016 for abuse at St Ninian's.

n: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
d: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.

n: US diocesan bankruptcies and settlements
who: US Catholic dioceses (Portland, Tucson, Spokane, San Diego, Davenport, Milwaukee, Albany and others)
cover: Milwaukee: Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with Vatican approval, moved $57 million into a cemetery trust, which kept it from victims; released files showed priests moved without telling police
d: Starting with Portland in 2004, at least 13 US dioceses filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy by 2023 under abuse claims. US dioceses have paid about $4 billion to roughly 17,000 victims since the 1980s. In Milwaukee, which filed in 2011 after paying $29 million on about 200 cases, released documents showed abusive priests were moved between assignments without notifying law enforcement.

n: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cover: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements
d: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.

n: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cover: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022
d: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.

n: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta
who: Archdiocese of Olomouc; Archbishop Jan Graubner (alleged failure to report)
cover: Archbishop Graubner allegedly did not report him and moved him between parishes
d: In 2000–2001 Fr František Merta was found guilty of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner allegedly failed to report him and moved him between parishes when problems arose.

n: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
place: San Ramón de la Nueva Orán, Salta
who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cover: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019
d: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.

n: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cover: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.
d: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.

n: Southern Baptist Convention — 'Abuse of Faith' investigation
place: Southern Baptist churches nationwide (most convicted offenders in Texas)
who: Southern Baptist Convention churches
d: The Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News published 'Abuse of Faith' on 10–11 February 2019. They found about 380 Southern Baptist ministers and volunteers had faced allegations of sexual misconduct over the previous 20 years, with more than 700 victims. Many pleaded guilty or were convicted, more from Texas than any other state.

n: Jehovah's Witnesses — Royal Commission Case Study 29
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Australia (Jehovah's Witnesses)
cover: None of the 1,006 alleged perpetrators recorded since 1950 was reported to police by the church. The 'two-witness rule' required two witnesses before elders' judicial committees could act, blocking 125 allegations; 401 members were expelled after internal hearings and 230 later readmitted.
d: At hearings in July–August 2015, the Royal Commission was told the Watch Tower Society's files held 1,006 alleged perpetrators of child sexual abuse since 1950, including 579 confessions, and that none had been reported to secular authorities. The Commission referred 514 alleged perpetrators to police. Its November 2016 report found the organisation did not respond adequately to child sexual abuse and that its two-witness rule showed a serious lack of understanding of abuse.

n: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
who: FLDS, Bountiful community
d: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.

n: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
d: On 19 June 2015 the High Court (A v Watchtower Bible and Tract Society [2015] EWHC 1722 (QB)) awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable. Separately, in July 2014 Barry congregation elder Mark Sewell was found guilty of eight sex offences including rape and sentenced to 14 years; a church judicial committee had earlier cleared him after the women reported him, and victims said other elders told them not to 'gossip' about the attacks.

n: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cover: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.
d: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.

n: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries — leader convicted of transporting girls across state lines
who: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries
d: On 24 July 2009 a federal jury convicted Tony Alamo on all 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; women testified he had taken them as 'wives' when they were children, some as young as 9. On 13 November 2009 he was sentenced to 175 years and fined $250,000. In 2013 federal authorities moved against 27 properties held by members to collect $2.5 million restitution. He died in custody in 2017.

n: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
place: Pakistan (cases in Kehrore Pakka, Mansehra, Punjab)
who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
cover: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.
d: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.

n: Salvation Army boys' homes — Australia
place: Bexley and Goulburn (NSW); Indooroopilly and Riverview (Queensland); Victoria
who: The Salvation Army (Australia)
cover: The Royal Commission heard that officers accused of abuse were moved interstate.
d: The Salvation Army sheltered about 30,000 Australian children from the 1940s to the 1980s and apologised in 2006 for abuse that may have occurred. Private settlements totalling A$15.5 million for 474 cases in Victoria were reported in 2013. In January–February 2014 the Royal Commission's Case Study 5 examined abuse at Bexley Boys' Home, Gill Memorial Home (Goulburn), Alkira (Indooroopilly) and Riverview Training Farm, and how accused officers were investigated and transferred.

n: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
who: Gloriavale Christian Community
cover: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.
d: Founder Neville Cooper ('Hopeful Christian') was sentenced in December 1995 to five years in prison on three charges of indecent assault against a young woman, after an earlier conviction on 10 counts involving five young complainants was overturned on appeal. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled that three former members had been employees from age six, doing 'strenuous, difficult and sometimes dangerous' work. Leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to indecently assaulting six girls and young women between 2002 and 2022, resigned as leader, and on 12 December 2025 was jailed for 26 months.

n: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
d: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on 3 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor, production of child pornography and human trafficking. On 3 June 2022, days before trial, he pleaded guilty to three counts involving minors (two of forcible oral copulation and one lewd act on a 15-year-old), and on 8 June 2022 was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty to four counts in 2020. In October 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him for producing and possessing child pornography involving a 16-year-old follower.

n: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
who: Lev Tahor
d: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.

n: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
d: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.
